candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor clients for potential complications associated with treatments and procedures, recognize changes in assessment findings, and implement measures that reduce complication risk.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postoperative/postpartum surveillance after cesarean birth
candidate.educational_objective: After cesarean birth, integrate routine postpartum surveillance with postoperative assessment of the incision, pain, bowel/bladder function, and mobility, and promote ambulation when clinically appropriate to support recovery and reduce complication risk.

options.A: Assess the incision, uterine fundus, lochia, pain, bowel and bladder function, and extremities; assist with ambulation when clinically appropriate and permitted.
options.B: Focus assessment on the abdominal incision because uterine tone and lochia are not clinically relevant after a cesarean birth.
options.C: Keep the client on bed rest until discharge to protect the incision and avoid provoking postoperative pain.
options.D: Delay incision assessment until discharge teaching unless the client first reports drainage or wound pain.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. A client who has had a cesarean birth requires both routine postpartum assessment and additional postoperative assessment. Current NCBI nursing guidance includes evaluation of the uterine fundus, lochia, bladder, bowel function, extremities, pain, and the cesarean dressing/incision. Early ambulation is also encouraged when clinically appropriate because it supports postoperative recovery and circulation. B is incorrect because cesarean birth does not eliminate the risk of uterine atony or postpartum hemorrhage; fundal and lochia assessment remain essential. C is incorrect because routine prolonged bed rest is not recommended and can impede recovery. D is incorrect because the incision is assessed during hospitalization for dressing condition, approximation, and signs of infection rather than only when symptoms are volunteered or at discharge.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Post-cesarean nursing care combines routine postpartum assessment with surgical-incision and postoperative assessment, pain management and clinically appropriate early mobility; fundal and lochia assessment remain necessary after cesarean birth.
